newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Legal hitch delays launch of Europe's newest bourse.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Legal hitch delays launch of Europe's newest bourse.

text.p: Blank screens greeted share dealers on Monday on Easdaq, Europe's newest equity market, as a legal hurdle prevented trading on the scheduled opening day.
But Easdaq's backers remained confident the delayed start would not prevent the market in small company stocks from flourishing.
They predicted there would be active dealing around the middle of October.
"Obviously we would have loved to have companies trading on the first day but the key thing is we have all the systems working," Easdaq spokesman Chris Pickles told Reuters.
"We should have 15 companies by Christmas, which puts us well on target for meeting the goal of 50 companies by the end of the first year," Pickles added.
Easdaq (European Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation) is a pan-European small cap market modelled on the United States' Nasdaq exchange.

Easdaq's aim is to do for European high-tech firms what Nasdaq has done for more than 5,000 U.S. companies -- encourage venture capital to pump money into small, adventurous firms that find it difficult to gain acceptance in traditional bourses.
Based in Brussels, but available on screen to traders throughout Europe, Easdaq targets European companies already listed on Nasdaq as well as new issues.

Companies known to be seeking admission are Belgian bio-tech firm Innogenetics, Belgian software firm Artwork Systems, German software firm Creatix, U.S. clinical testing firm UniHolding Corp, British vehicle management firm Pride Automotive Group and Canadian bio-tech firm DynaMotive Technologies.
The last three are already listed on Nasdaq.
However, the rules governing admissions were not approved by Belgium's finance ministry until last Thursday, which prevented listings being approved before Monday's launch.
Applications for listings must legally be approved by Easdaq and Belgium's regulatory Banking and Finance Commission before quotation in any issue can begin.
"We expect to have several shares quoted before the end of (October)," said a trader at KB Securities in Brussels, one of many firms vying to become Easdaq brokers.
Each company listed on Easdaq must be supported by two market makers.
Pickles said it was likely the first issue on Easdaq would be a Nasdaq-quoted European company seeking a dual listing rather than a company issuing new capital.
Initial public offerings (IPOs) would follow later. "We would never have recommended them on day one," he said.
Despite the procedural delay in approving Easdaq's rules, no companies waiting in the pipeline had cancelled their plans, he said.
